lesson.title: The three accent marks
lesson.objective: Recognize acute, grave and circumflex, identify their possible syllable positions, and recognize the usual change from final acute to grave in connected text.
lesson.approachReason: The shapes of the marks and a map of their syllable positions make the distinctions visible before the learner applies them to Greek words.

blocks.heading: Three shapes to recognize
blocks.body:
Look at the mark above each vowel: ά has an **acute**, which rises to the right; ὰ has a **grave**, which slopes the other way; ᾶ has a **circumflex**, shown here as a little wave.

Some Greek fonts draw the circumflex as a curved cap instead. Recognize the mark's shape before worrying about how to pronounce the word.
blocks.example: The vowel is just a carrier in these examples: your target is the little mark above it.

hints: Does the mark look like a diagonal stroke or a curved wave?
blocks.retry: Ignore the letters for a moment. The wave-shaped mark is the circumflex; the two diagonal strokes are acute and grave.

blocks.heading: Read the map from the word's end
blocks.body:
Count backward from the end: **last**, **second-last**, **third-last**. The acute can stand on any of these three syllables; the grave only on the last; the circumflex only on the last or second-last.

These are the outer limits, not a guarantee that every position works in every word. A circumflex needs a long vowel or a diphthong—a pair of vowels functioning together—and vowel length imposes further restrictions that you will study later.
blocks.example: In λόγος, the acute is on the second-last syllable. In δῶρον, the circumflex is on the second-last syllable. In θεοῦ, the circumflex is on the last.

hints: Check the third-last position on the map.
Which mark has the widest position range?
blocks.retry: Imagine three boxes at the end of a word. Only the acute's position map reaches the third-last box.

blocks.heading: Watch the final acute change shape
blocks.body:
The grave usually appears when a word with a final acute is followed by another word without intervening punctuation. Compare **καλός.** at a stop with **καλὸς φίλος** in connected text: the accent stays on the last syllable, but its shape changes.

A final acute normally remains acute before punctuation. There are exceptions to the connected-text rule, which you will meet later; for now, notice that the grave is not a mark you can freely move to another syllable.
blocks.example: Visual change: ό → ὸ. Same vowel, same syllable, different accent mark.

hints: Which word has an acute on its last syllable?
Change that mark's shape without moving it. A grave cannot stand on the second-last syllable.
blocks.retry: Change the final acute of καλός to a grave. Leave the acute of φίλος alone: it is on the second-last syllable, not the last.

activities.title: Sort by shape, not by vowel
activities.prompt: Drag each accented vowel to its accent name. The vowel letter changes, but the three shapes stay recognizable.
activities.reveal: Acute and grave are opposite-sloping strokes. The circumflex is the wave or curved cap, regardless of the vowel underneath.

activities.title: The last three syllables
activities.prompt: Tap each accent node and trace its links to the syllable positions. Find the mark that reaches farthest back, then the mark that reaches only the last syllable.
activities.reveal: The acute reaches the last three syllables, the circumflex the last two, and the grave only the last. These are maximum position ranges; other rules can narrow the choices.

nodes.label: Acute: ά
nodes.detail: Can stand on the last, second-last or third-last syllable.

nodes.label: Grave: ὰ
nodes.detail: Can stand only on the last syllable.

nodes.label: Circumflex: ᾶ
nodes.detail: Can stand on the last or second-last syllable, but never the third-last.

nodes.label: Third-last
nodes.detail: Count three syllables back from the end. Of the three accent marks, only the acute can reach this position.

nodes.label: Second-last
nodes.detail: The syllable immediately before the last. An acute or a circumflex can occur here, but not a grave.

nodes.label: Last
nodes.detail: The final syllable. All three marks can occur here, subject to the other accent rules.

questions.question: While reading δῶρον, you pause to identify the mark above ω. Which mark are you seeing?
questions.explanation: The curved, wave-like mark above ω is a circumflex. An acute or grave would be a diagonal stroke.

questions.question: A practice card highlights the third-last syllable of a four-syllable word. Without yet checking vowel length, which accent is the only one whose position range can reach that syllable?
options: Both the acute and the circumflex
questions.explanation: Only the acute can stand on the third-last syllable. The circumflex reaches at most the second-last, and the grave only the last.

questions.question: You join καλός and φίλος into one phrase with no punctuation between them. Keeping each word's accent on its original syllable, which printing follows the usual connected-text rule?
questions.explanation: The final acute of καλός becomes grave before φίλος. The acute in φίλος stays unchanged because it is on the second-last syllable; a grave could not stand there.

sources.title: Accents and Accentuation | Dickinson College Commentaries

problems: The position-map activity mainly asks learners to inspect supplied links rather than construct or predict the permitted positions, limiting its cognitive demand.
Checks do not directly test the circumflex's long-vowel/diphthong requirement or its exclusion from the third-last syllable independently of the acute-range question.
Some hints and retry explanations disclose the answer rather than offering a genuinely different route to understanding, especially in the final check.
